**Direct answer:** Einstein never won a Nobel Prize for general relativity, so the question rests on a false premise. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded in 1922, for his services to theoretical physics and especially the photoelectric effect.

**Claims and sources**

- Einstein's Nobel citation reads "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect." It doesn't mention relativity.
  - https://nobel-prize.net/en/topics/einstein-and-the-prize/
  - https://www.kroneckerwallis.com/the-photoelectric-effect-why-einstein-won-the-nobel-prize/ (this was a search result I didn't open, so it's only a snippet-level source)

- The prize is the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. The committee held it back in 1921 and awarded it retroactively in November 1922.
  - https://nobel-prize.net/en/topics/einstein-and-the-prize/

- Relativity was passed over because parts of the committee doubted it or wanted experimental confirmation. Planck nominated Einstein for relativity, and Oseen proposed the photoelectric effect as the safer basis.
  - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.13519 (this was a search-result summary only. The PDF didn't render when I tried to open it, so I couldn't check the wording directly.)

**Caveats:** I couldn't open nobelprize.org, which returned a 403. The citation wording and the 1921/1922 timing come from nobel-prize.net, a secondary site, and the committee-motive details come from search summaries I couldn't check directly.
